title: First all-night job, lessons, Laine and Tom Brown, then Chicago and Lake Geneva
summary: He recalls his father's dance music, his first all-night job, reading lessons with Tony Maggio, playing with Jack Laine and Tom Brown, and going to Chicago alone where the Petrello brothers got him work.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: And did your father play ragtime?

Well, in them days there was what you call, it wasn't ragtime in them days. My father did. You know, it was dance fans, you know, but there wasn't no pep, you know? It was a regular, legitimate resistance, you see? Of course, they played with what was called ragtime in them days, but none of them was out there the Negroes. You see, my daddy gave it up. My daddy gave up music out when I was about ten years old, you see? You know, I'll never forget I was a young kid. First time I stood out all night, played with a bunch of men old enough to be my daddy, you know? And, uh, played a dance, never forget the song as I was out of there, right on the Dominion and the Mall Street, by St. John. And I didn't come home that night next morning, we were getting home until 7 o'clock that morning. My daddy was worried. When I went home, I grabbed my corner and break it up and said, that's what you're going to do and I'll stay out all night? Because in them days and these days, it didn't 4 o'clock, 1 o'clock, it was plenty. But, you know, I was playing with a bunch of old, old fellows, you know? A bunch of old me to be my daddy, and Jesus, God, the man that we do will be. And after that night, I thought I was tops. Everybody started hiring me. All them old fellows would come get me, you see? Because I could take them. I took lessons from a man by the name of, uh, uh, Tony Maggio. And, uh, I took music lessons, reading lessons. I went to him, he was a wonderful musician. I went to him to learn how to read, you see? So, I went with my trumpet there and he seen what I could do with a trumpet. I could do more with a trumpet than he could. He said, yeah, he just, I used to amuse him. Because he could play, but he never could fake, you know? Memorize. He was, I'd amuse him. And he just take and sit down there and say, you come in and take dresses. The only thing I could do is give me music lessons. Come here without your trumpet. And I went to him and said. We were having salt, salt bed music. You know, singing. Singing salt bed music. Then I got soldier. Oh, then Jacqueline caught ahold of me. Oh, well he caught me, man. Then from there, what was Tom Brown? Tom Brown grabbed ahold of me. After Tom Brown grabbed ahold of me. Oh, after Tom Brown grabbed me, let's see, I'm trying to find, I went away. No, came down, came back again. Stood a while, went back up north, went back around Chicago. Worked with something, you know, the garage. And then most of the time, that I was in Chicago, you know, a lot of these boys down here would leave here and they'd go up nothing else and they'd get the swell there, you know what I mean? They'd want to quit, but, if you follow with them there, it wasn't like today. You know, you know, you're a man go off for you $20 or 15 hours a week more, they'd quit, gone. But we had to do that though, smart. See? And, when I went up there, I went by myself. Most of these organized bands went up there together. Then when they got up there, one fella wanted to get this fella, you know, break the band up and move naturally, and they made a fool of these. See, the only one stuck together was the Nicola Rocca. See, you heard of that. For me, when I went alone. And I didn't have no trouble with all of them. I got a job by the way. Oh. And then I got to get, Jimmy Petrello was president of the Chicago local, and his brother, Caesar. Caesar Petrello, the trombone player. So I was up in Chicago. And I was up to local. I didn't put my transfer card in. So, a fella says, you want a job for the night? I says, yeah. They had a job at Lake Geneva. I said, where in the devil is Lake Geneva? I don't know. I said, finally. He said, well, I'll pick you up. He picked me up. And I went on a job. Bunch of men sitting down there, about 10, 11 men. Never grew a horse, nothing like that. Oh. They introduced me. I sat down. Put the real voice number. I forgot those blood. Never get as wrong as I live. I was kind of shaky, you know? People were a strange man, you know what I mean? Yeah. I played the voice number, the second number. The trombone player sitting next to me was Caesar Petrello, Jimmy Petrello's brother. He put his trombone on. He says, what's your name again? I told him, he said, where you from? I said, I'm not going to be a man. I'm not going to be a man. I'm not going to be a man.
I'm not going to be a man. I'm not going to be a man. I'm not going to be a man. I'm not going to be a man.
